title: Mahendra Pratap Singh v. State of U.P. & 8 Others
coram: Arun Tandon, J. & Raghvendra Kumar, J.
disposition: Writ dismissed; CGRF order of 16.9.2016 stands; liberty to challenge the revised bill under Clause 6.5
headnote: Where a consumer who paid nothing on a residential connection for 31 years challenges a CGRF order rejecting his complaint against a demand and recovery certificate, and the licensee has since issued a revised bill which the consumer has not challenged, the writ court is not the proper forum to test the correctness of the assessment. Grievance as to the demand is to be pursued under Clause 6.5 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. A recovery certificate cannot be challenged in writ when the underlying bill — the basic order — is not under challenge; a consequential order cannot be subjected to challenge if the basic order is not. Finding no error in the CGRF order dated 16.9.2016, the Court dismissed the writ, discharged any interim order, and left the petitioner at liberty to challenge the revised bill under Clause 6.5. It did not examine the departmental ledger or decide whether the revised bill was correctly computed on average consumption.
facts:
Mahendra Pratap Singh challenged the 16 September 2016 order of the Electricity Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum, Aligarh. He held a residential 1 KW connection (No. 027516), sanctioned and energised on 25 July 1985. An earlier 11 KW connection had been permanently disconnected on 14 August 1998. He paid nothing on the 1 KW load for 31 years. A demand/recovery of about Rs. 3,31,940 followed. His Clause 6.5 objection under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 was rejected. He complained to the CGRF at Agra (Case No. 761 of 2016/Mainpuri), later transferred to Aligarh.

During the Forum hearing the licensee issued a revised bill dated 6 January 2016 for Rs. 1,69,784, and the District Magistrate, Mainpuri, issued a revised recovery certificate dated 30 January 2016. The petitioner deposited Rs. 18,000 on 4 March 2016 and nothing thereafter. The Forum rejected the complaint because he had challenged neither the revised bill nor the recovery certificate. In the writ he asked the Court to call for the departmental ledger, saying the revised bill was on average consumption rather than actual readings.

holding_units.topic: writ not the forum for correctness of an assessment; recovery certificate not challengeable unless the bill is; liberty to Clause 6.5
holding_units.question: Where the consumer challenges a CGRF rejection of a complaint against a demand and recovery certificate, without having challenged the revised bill, should the writ court examine the assessment, or is the consumer to proceed under Clause 6.5?
holding_units.holding: The writ court is not the proper forum to challenge the assessment. Grievance as to the correctness of the demand is to be taken under Clause 6.5 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, and it is for that authority to examine the aspects the consumer raises. Without a challenge to the bill, a challenge to the recovery certificate does not arise: if the basic order is not under challenge, the consequential order cannot be subjected to challenge. The Court found no error in the CGRF order dated 16.9.2016, dismissed the writ, discharged any interim order, and clarified that the petitioner remains at liberty to challenge the revised bill under Clause 6.5 before the appropriate authority.
holding_units.qualifier: A Clause 6.5 objection to the original demand of about Rs. 3,31,940 had already been rejected. The liberty granted is to challenge the revised bill dated 6.1.2016.

principle_tags.application: The writ against the CGRF rejection was dismissed because the writ court is not the proper forum to test the assessment. The consumer was left at liberty to challenge the revised bill under Clause 6.5.

Correctness of the demand, including the contention that the revised bill was on average consumption without ledger readings, was held to lie in the Clause 6.5 procedure before the concerned authority.
The Court held that without a challenge to the bill, a challenge to the recovery certificate does not arise; the bill is the basic order and the recovery certificate the consequential order.

authorities.proposition: Cited with two other Supreme Court decisions for the proposition that if the basic order is not under challenge, a consequential order cannot be subjected to challenge — applied here so that the recovery certificate could not be challenged without a challenge to the bill.
